value: B: default subscriptions are predefined email notifications. C: personal notifications are managed by and for one user, not sent to an outside service. A: a custom email subscription emails organisation or team members, not an outside service.
reason: 'Personal notifications still arrive by email' is not in about-notifications, which only lists Personal notifications against the User role and says notifications go 'through email or service hook, based on the delivery properties defined in the subscription'.

value: What do the code tile and build history widgets show?
reason: The front promises release widgets too, but the back covers only code tiles and build history; the dashboards overview names the deployment status widget only in image alt text.

value: Azure Boards makes the change through a GitHub commit and pull request, which you merge in GitHub to see the badge.
reason: 'Only appears when ... the linked pull request is still open' is not in install-github-app, which says Azure Boards 'Creates a GitHub pull request to merge the changes to the README file', then 'Select Merge pull request in GitHub ... open the README file to verify the badge was added.'

value: The first hides changes from reviewers; the second shows changes that folder-mapped policies then fail to check.
reason: The old explanation said both risks come from the Files tab not showing the true changes, but the second risk is changes that 'are displayed in the Files tab, but they might not trigger branch policies that are mapped to folder changes' (merging-with-squash, Potential security risks).

value:
A) On, as Optional
B) On, as Required
C) Off, with a comment resolution policy instead
D) Off, with a reminder in the team wiki
reason: Choice D ('On, with a path filter of `*`') and its explanation assume the linked work items policy takes a path filter; branch-policies documents path filters for build, status check and reviewer policies but not for Check for linked work items.

value: B blocks merging until work items are linked. C doesn’t check work items at all. D gives no warning in the pull request itself.
reason: Goes with the new choice D; the old 'D still requires links for every file' rested on an undocumented path filter.

value: B limits merge commits, not who is exempt. C: people with admin permissions can always push, whatever the restrictions. D makes the branch read-only, stopping every commit rather than making admins meet the review rule.
reason: 'Read-only for everyone' overstates: by default a rule's restrictions, including Lock branch, 'don't apply to people with admin permissions'. Source: 'Locking a branch will make the branch read-only and ensures that no commits can be made to the branch.'

value: With several hundred developers completing over 200 pull requests a day in one repository, Microsoft says a deployment queue would leave them waiting.
reason: 'Hundreds of pull requests a day' overstates the Learn page (tier C), which says teams of 'several hundred developers ... can complete over 200 pull requests into the main branch per day'.

value: Annotated tags record who tagged, when and why; the web portal creates only these, so lightweight tags come from the Git command line.
reason: 'Both kinds in Visual Studio' clashes with the same article's Create tag section: 'You can only create annotated tags in the web portal or Visual Studio. To create a lightweight tag, you can use Git command line.'

value: A research group wants large data files kept out of Git’s objects and synced to its own server over rsync, with only stock Python and rsync installed. Which tool fits?
reason: 'Nothing but Python installed' contradicts git-fat's needs and the scenario's own rsync: 'depends only on stock Python and rsync'.
